title: Lust and chastity
hook: chastity means love that respects people, whether single or married
tomorrow: works of mercy for the body

segments.voice: Yesterday, gluttony and temperance: Esau and the red stew. Your line was eat with thanks. Did you slow down for one meal? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

It's evening in Jerusalem, in the season when kings go out to battle. But King David has stayed home. He gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof, and from up there, the King James text says, he saw a woman bathing, "and the woman was very beautiful to look upon." The next words are quiet and terrible: "David sent and enquired after the woman." He learns her name, Bathsheba. He learns she is married, to one of his own soldiers, away at the war. And he sends for her anyway. A look, then a question, then a summons. Today: lust and chastity.

Notice how the story moves. David doesn't start with a crime. He starts with a look, and the look becomes a plan, and the plan treats Bathsheba as something a king can send for. In the whole scene she barely speaks. She is acted upon. That's the heart of what Christian teaching means by lust. Not desire itself; the Bible celebrates desire, and gives a whole book, the Song of Songs, to lovers longing for each other. Lust is desire that turns a person into a thing to be used. Jesus takes it inward, to the look: "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." He moves it from the hands to the heart, where it starts. Chastity is the answer, and it can sound like nothing but a no. It isn't only that. In Christian teaching chastity is for everyone, single or married. For someone single, churches teach it as waiting; for someone married, as faithfulness to one person. In both, the root is the same: love that respects the whole person. Why the whole person? Because of the very first page of the Bible. "God created man in his own image." In Christian teaching, every person you see carries that image. And Paul tells the Corinthians, "your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost." Not a thing. A temple. Christians differ on many questions about sex and marriage, and churches teach different things on some of them. But the lines from Genesis and from Paul point one way: a person is never an object. David's story doesn't end on the roof. The prophet Nathan comes to him later, and David hears what he's done.

Here's the practice: treat everyone as a whole person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a few people you'll see or scroll past today. A coworker, a stranger on the street, someone on a screen. For each one, slowly add what you can't see: a mother somewhere, a bad night, a favorite song, a name. Let each one become a whole life, not a picture. If you pray, you can hold Genesis in mind: made in the image of God. The bell holds the time.
Lust and chastity. Desire that uses a person, and love that respects the whole person, whether single or married.
Your line: people, not things. Today, when your eyes land on someone, on a street or on a screen, give them their whole life back in your mind. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

notes: Sensitive day. The David and Bathsheba story is told with David as the one acting; Bathsheba is not blamed. 'She barely speaks' refers to 2 Samuel 11, where her only words are 'I am with child' (11:5). Confirm.
Genesis 1:27 is quoted with an ellipsis ('God created man in his own image... male and female created he them'); the sources line quotes the first clause. Confirm the ellipsis is acceptable.

'Christians differ on many questions about sex and marriage, and churches teach different things on some of them. But the lines from Genesis and from Paul point one way: a person is never an object.' Keeper to confirm.
Chastity for single and married people (waiting; faithfulness) is stated as church teaching in general; confirm the description is fair across Protestant, Orthodox and Catholic teaching.
The Song of Songs is described as a book of lovers' longing; readings differ (literal and allegorical). Confirm.
